title: 2.1 Other Related Work
use_cases: Use when benchmarking LLM-based semantic inference against traditional lexical similarity measures
Implement when developing metrics for quantifying text cohesion and coherence through isotopy density
Configure when designing system prompts for structured textual semantic extraction
Use when comparing stylistic and grammatical dimensions between human writing and LLM-generated text
Implement when moving from simple heuristics to intermediate semantic representations for genre detection
content:
There are obvious connections between distributional semantics, corpus linguistics and the textual approach to semantics we are advocating here. Uchida (2024) analyzed text generated by older LLM such as GPT-3.5 from a corpus linguistics perspective, comparing collocations to corpus data. Reinhart et al. (2025) used corpus-based grammatical and stylistic dimensions to compare human writing to LLM text generation. However, the above works still relies heavily on vocabulary usage Durward and Thomson (2024), and are relatively underspecified in semantic terms, in particular on higher-level aspects such as genre detection, which is still based on simple heuristics rather than intermediate semantic representations Rastier (1997). Although the focus of our work is not explicitly on textual cohesion, it is worth noting that many of the concepts discussed have been associated to text cohesion which in textual semantics is based on the construction of isotopies. Moreover, notwithstanding debates on the relationship between cohesion and coherence, in textual semantics the former determines the latter, for instance through association between isotopies and discourse topics Rastier (1997). In this work, we will only be concerned with the initial step of isotopy construction as a textual semantic representation. For the identification of recurring semantic units, LLM-based inference substitutes itself to previous lexical similarity measures that have been used in text cohesion or coherence studies, several of which having been compared in Lapata et al. (2005) Budanitsky and Hirst (2006), or even approaches that have incorporated distributional aspects Marathe and Hirst (2010) Aletras and Stevenson (2013). At the other end of the processing pipeline, the quantification of isotopies’ properties can be performed by adapting metrics developed for lexical chains such as span Feng et al. (2009) and density Hollingsworth (2008) providing a simpler and consistent approach than more complex metrics such as CohMetric Seals and Shalin (2023), LongWanjuan Liu et al. (2024b), or BERT-based metrics for cohesion He et al. (2022).
